description: Question: Germany uses about as much electricity at 1 pm as at 8 pm, so why is the wholesale price often below zero at 1 pm and at its highest at 8 pm? Data: two months (May and June 2026) of quarter-hourly public net generation, load and residual load for Germany, and the DE-LU day-ahead price, from Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE; generation from ENTSO-E, prices from Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, CC BY 4.0). Idea: the merit order. A power market sorts plants by their running (marginal) cost: wind, sun and run-of-river cost almost nothing per MWh, lignite and nuclear little, hard coal more, gas the most; the plant that is needed last to meet demand sets the uniform price for everyone. So the price follows the residual load (load minus wind and solar: what dispatchable plants must cover), not the load. Steps (Polars and SQL): the source arrays to rows; one row per quarter-hour with the price; hourly means; the hours binned by residual load (the empirical supply curve: median price, 10-90% band, and which plants run in each bin); the average day; least-squares fits of the price on load, on residual load and on wind+solar; and the slope in three ranges of residual load. The aha: plotted against load the price is a cloud (R² 0.03 over 1,464 hours); against residual load it is a rising curve (R² 0.70): at or below zero where wind and sun cover the whole load, a steep step as the first dispatchable plants are needed, a gentle plateau from 20 to 35 GW where lignite, coal and imports fill in (about 2 EUR/MWh per GW), and steep again above 35 GW where gas and pumped hydro run (about 11 EUR/MWh per GW, up to 666 EUR/MWh). The midday 'duck' in the residual load and the evening price peak are the same curve seen through the clock. Caveats: two months of one bidding zone; the price is the day-ahead auction (intraday and balancing prices differ); hourly means smooth quarter-hour spikes; fuel and CO₂ prices (which move the whole curve) and cross-border flows are not modelled; negative prices come from must-run plants and subsidies paid per MWh, not from the merit order alone. Next: change start and end to a winter month (the curve moves up with gas prices), or the bidding zone (bzn=FR, NO2, SE3) to see a hydro- or nuclear-shaped curve.
name: The merit order: why sunny noons are cheap
